alt: Step-by-step role of the loss function in a deep network: input, forward propagation gives a predicted output of 185 g, the actual output is 180 g, the loss is 5 g, backpropagation sends the error back, weights are updated and the process repeats until the loss is small.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: MAE example with 4 samples: actual 180, 200, 160, 150 and predicted 185, 195, 170, 145 give absolute errors 5, 5, 10, 5. MAE equals 25 divided by 4, which is 6.25 g.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: MSE squares every error before averaging. An error of 2 g gives a penalty of 4 and an error of 20 g gives a penalty of 400, so larger errors get a much higher penalty.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: MSE example with 4 samples: errors minus 5, 5, minus 10, 5 give squared errors 25, 25, 100, 25. MSE equals 175 divided by 4, which is 43.75.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: MAE versus MSE on a number line: MAE uses the absolute difference and gives equal importance to every error, MSE uses the squared difference and gives a higher penalty to large errors. Minus 10 becomes 10 in MAE and 100 in MSE.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Two farms with the same error of 10 fruits: Farm A actual 100 and predicted 110, Farm B actual 1000 and predicted 1010. The same error is significant for Farm A and very small for Farm B, so they are not equally wrong.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Binary cross entropy formula BCE equals minus (y log y-hat plus (1 minus y) log (1 minus y-hat)), with symbols and intuition: if y is 1 a high y-hat gives low loss, if y is 0 a low y-hat gives low loss.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Good versus bad predictions for binary cross entropy: actual 1 with prediction 0.95 gives very small loss, 0.50 medium, 0.10 very large. Actual 0 with prediction 0.05 gives very small loss, 0.50 medium, 0.90 very large.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Hinge loss versus squared hinge loss for a margin y times y-hat: margin 2 and 1 give 0 and 0, margin 0.5 gives 0.5 and 0.25, margin minus 1 gives 2 and 4, margin minus 2 gives 3 and 9.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Categorical cross entropy: CCE equals minus the sum of y_i log y-hat_i, with y_i the one-hot actual class and y-hat_i the softmax probability. Example: actual Orange is 0, 0, 1, 0 and predicted probabilities are 0.05, 0.10, 0.80, 0.05, so the loss is small.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Sparse categorical cross entropy uses integer labels (Apple 0, Banana 1, Orange 2, Mango 3) instead of one-hot vectors, which saves memory and simplifies training.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: KL divergence compares two probability distributions: the actual distribution P (apple 0.70, banana 0.20, orange 0.10) and the predicted distribution Q (0.60, 0.25, 0.15).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Quick guide to which loss to use: regression with a linear output uses MSE or MAE, binary classification with sigmoid uses binary cross entropy, multi-class with softmax uses categorical cross entropy, imbalanced classification uses focal loss or class-weighted CE, outliers use MAE or Huber loss.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How to choose a loss function: MSE or MAE for regression, binary cross entropy for binary classification, categorical cross entropy for multi-class. The simple training flow goes input data, model, prediction, actual, loss, update weights, repeat until loss is small.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Squared error loss (MSE): L equals 1 over n times the sum of (y minus y-hat) squared, used for regression. Its curve is a parabola, and an example table with true value 3 gives squared errors 1, 1, 4 and 4.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: Cross entropy loss for binary classification with its curve for y equals 1 and y equals 0 against the predicted probability, and an example table: true 1 with 0.9 gives 0.105, true 1 with 0.1 gives 2.303, true 0 with 0.9 gives 2.303, true 0 with 0.1 gives 0.105.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: Precision equals TP divided by (TP plus FP). Recall equals TP divided by (TP plus FN).
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: F1 score equals 2 times precision times recall divided by (precision plus recall), the harmonic average of precision and recall.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut
